background.definition: A dental abscess is a localized collection of pus in the teeth, supporting structures of the teeth, or gums. There are two types of dental abscesses: periapical and periodontal. Periapical abscesses originate in the dental pulp. Periodontal abscesses originate in the supporting structures between the tooth and the gum.

list.listitem: Dentists estimate that approximately 5% of their patients present each year with dental infections.
In a prospective study of nearly 900 adults, approximately 2% received endodontic treatment per year, mainly for abscess.
The lifetime prevalence of abscess is between 5% and 46%.
Among 256 teeth extracted for pain or swelling, 35% were periapical abscess, 50% were granulomas, and 15% were cysts.
Approximately 60% of patients have severe bone loss and 30% have moderate bone loss visible on dental x-rays.
Treating periodontal disease slightly improves control of diabetes (low quality evidence).
Most dental abscesses are polymicrobial in origin, predominantly anaerobes.

Causative organisms include Peptostreptococcus species, Actinomyces species, Streptococcus species, Fusobacterium nucleatum, Prevotella species, Tannerella forsythia, Campylobacter rectus, and Porphyromonas gingivalis.

Periodontitis causes separation of the periodontal ligament from the tooth, resulting in a pocket. Periodontal pockets are difficult to clean, allowing bacteria to invade and multiply, leading to inflammation and periodontal abscess formation.
Dental caries erode the enamel and dentine layers, allowing bacteria to invade the pulp, causing pulpitis, which can progress to necrosis and periapical abscess formation.

Children and adults should have routine dental examinations every 6 months and properly care for their teeth and gums (brushing, flossing, and rinsing). Weak evidence supports flossing to prevent gingivitis. C

Pantomogram (panoramic extraoral radiograph) is useful to show the extent of the abscess, but it is usually only available in dental offices.

All patients with dental abscess should have definitive treatment by a dental practitioner.

Primary care physicians should reduce the patient's pain while he or she awaits dental care and should only use antibiotics in patients with signs of systemic illness or airway compromise, or in those with high risk.

In a recent meta-analysis of 8 clinical trials with 531 patients, 85% of control patients were free of pain and infection at the end of the studies compared with 75% of patients treated with antibiotics. Although patients taking antibiotics had slightly lower pain scores than control patients, the differences were not statistically significant.
When antibiotics are used, amoxicillin, metronidazole, erythromycin, or clindamycin for up to 5 days are recommended on the basis of expert opinion.
Suggestions for antibiotic dosing: penicillin V 500 mg every 6 hours, metronidazole 500 mg twice daily, clindamycin 300 mg every 8 hours, or amoxicillin 500 mg every 8 hours.

Only 13 of 29 (45%) patients with recent dental abscesses or with loss of gingival attachment who took doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 3 weeks had signs of recurrent periodontal disease compared with 15 of 19 (79%) patients taking placebo (NNT = 3; 95% CI, 2-18).
The most important and immediate step in treating a dental abscess is to mechanically incise and drain the abscess.

Periapical abscesses are normally managed by root canal treatment. If the infection persists despite root canal treatment, the dentist may have to extract the tooth or refer the patient to an oral surgeon for surgical removal of diseased tissue.
Periodontal abscesses are normally drained and the periodontal pocket is cleaned. Sometimes a referral to an oral surgeon may be needed for repeated infections.

Refer patients to the hospital and seek advice from an oral surgeon if the patient has high fever, cardiovascular compromise, dysphagia or swelling in the floor of the mouth, spreading infection, or if they are immunocompromised.
Dental abscesses persist until they are drained. C
Prognosis is good with treatment. C
Mortality is extremely rare, and it is usually secondary to airway compromise. There are no cases of death from sepsis secondary to dental abscess reported in the literature. C
